title: Fire: where the wax goes, and why burning loses nothing

summary.text: A log can weigh three kilograms and leave a handful of ash, so where did the rest go? Yet a tuft of steel wool does the opposite and gets heavier when it burns. Your child holds a cold plate over a flame and catches drops of water and black soot. They find out how the shape of the same paper changes how fast it burns, and they weigh burning steel wool on a homemade balance. They learn that burning is a chemical reaction in which the same atoms swap partners. They also learn why a blue flame is cleaner than a yellow one, why the Sun is not a fire, and how a flame's colour can tell us what a star is made of.
summary.art: A cold steel plate held above a tea-light flame, with clear drops of water and a patch of black soot on its underside, and a steel-wool balance made from a skewer in the background.

intro.hook: A grown-up lights a tea-light candle. A cold steel plate is held a hand's width above the flame for ten seconds. When the plate is lifted, its underside is wet with tiny drops and has a black smudge. The candle was burning, so how can it make water?
intro.text: Fire seems to use things up. A log turns into a pinch of ash, and a candle gets shorter and shorter. In this unit you catch what a flame really makes. You test what changes how fast something burns, and you weigh things before and after burning. Then you follow the idea out to your own breath, to the Sun, and to flames burning in space.
intro.art: A steel plate held over a candle flame, with drops of water on its underside and a thin black smudge of soot, and a child watching closely beside a grown-up.

outcomes: I can explain that burning is a chemical reaction in which a fuel joins with oxygen and makes new substances such as carbon dioxide, water and soot.
I can explain why the wax of a candle is not destroyed when it burns, and where it goes.
I can run a fair test that changes one thing at a time, and use the results to say what makes something burn faster or slower.
I can explain the difference between a yellow, sooty flame and a blue flame, and why a blue flame is safer.
I can explain why burning steel wool gets heavier but burning paper seems to get lighter.
I can explain how a fire can be put out, and why water is the wrong choice for a burning pan of oil.
I can say why the Sun is not a fire, and how a flame's colour helps scientists find out what stars are made of.
I can say how people once explained burning with phlogiston, and how weighing showed that idea was wrong.

terms.meaning: The scientific word for burning. A fuel joins with oxygen very fast and gives out heat and light.
terms.example: A gas stove burner is combustion of LPG.
terms.art: A blue ring of flame on a gas stove burner.

terms.meaning: A change in which the atoms of some substances come apart and join up in a new way to make different substances.
terms.example: Wax and oxygen change into carbon dioxide and water when a candle burns.
terms.art: Two small groups of coloured balls rearranging into two new groups, with an arrow between them.

terms.meaning: A new substance that a chemical reaction makes.
terms.example: Carbon dioxide and water vapour are two products of a burning candle.
terms.art: A candle flame with arrows pointing to labels for carbon dioxide, water vapour and soot.

terms.meaning: A colourless gas made when carbon joins with oxygen. It is heavier than air, and it does not burn.
terms.example: You breathe out carbon dioxide, and so does a burning candle.
terms.art: A child breathing out onto a mirror, with a small label for carbon dioxide.

terms.meaning: Water as an invisible gas. It turns back into drops of water when it touches something cold.
terms.example: A cold steel tumbler gets drops on the outside on a hot day.
terms.art: A cold steel tumbler with drops of water on its outside.

terms.meaning: Tiny black bits of unburnt carbon. They glow yellow inside a flame, and settle as a black powder when the flame meets something cold.
terms.example: A diya held under a steel plate leaves a black patch on it.
terms.art: A steel plate with a black soot patch over a small oil lamp.

terms.meaning: Burning with plenty of oxygen, so that all the carbon turns into carbon dioxide. The flame is blue and makes no soot.
terms.example: A gas stove with clean burners burns with a blue flame.
terms.art: A gas stove burner with a clean blue flame under a steel pan.

terms.meaning: Burning without enough oxygen, so some carbon is left as soot or as the poisonous gas carbon monoxide. The flame is yellow.
terms.example: A candle flame is yellow, and a steel plate held in it gets sooty.
terms.art: A yellow candle flame with a black patch on a spoon held in it.

terms.meaning: A poisonous gas with no colour and no smell. It forms when something carbon-rich burns without enough oxygen.
terms.example: A coal fire in a closed room can fill the room with carbon monoxide.
terms.art: A closed room with a glowing coal angithi in the middle and a warning sign on the door.

terms.meaning: The total area of the outside of something. Cutting a thing into small pieces gives it more surface area for the same weight.
terms.example: Thin shavings of wood have more surface than a whole log of the same weight.
terms.art: A whole log and a heap of wood shavings side by side on a table.

terms.meaning: Small, thin, dry pieces of fuel used to start a fire, because they catch quickly.
terms.example: Dry twigs and coconut fronds are used to light a chulha.
terms.art: A small pile of dry twigs and coconut fronds under a larger log.

terms.meaning: A substance made when a material joins with oxygen. Rust and the ash of burnt metal are oxides.
terms.example: Rust is iron joined with oxygen, and it weighs more than the iron did.
terms.art: A shiny iron nail beside a rusty iron nail.

terms.meaning: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of everything stays the same. Nothing is made and nothing is destroyed. The atoms are only rearranged.
terms.example: The mass of a candle plus the oxygen it uses equals the mass of the carbon dioxide and water it makes.
terms.art: A balance with a candle and a jar of air on one pan, and jars of gas on the other, both level.

terms.meaning: An invisible substance that chemists in the 1700s believed escaped from every burning thing. We now know it does not exist.
terms.example: People said wood burns because phlogiston leaves it.
terms.art: An old drawing of a burning log with a made-up cloud rising from it labelled phlogiston, crossed out.

terms.meaning: How the cells of a living body get energy from food and oxygen. It makes carbon dioxide and water, and it is a slow cousin of burning.
terms.example: When you run, your cells use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide.
terms.art: A child running, with arrows showing oxygen going in and carbon dioxide going out.

terms.meaning: Joining the tiny centres of atoms together so that they make a bigger atom and give out a huge amount of energy. The Sun shines this way.
terms.example: In the Sun, hydrogen joins together to make helium.
terms.art: The Sun with two small hydrogen atoms joining into one helium atom in a magnified circle.

explanations.definition: Burning is a chemical reaction in which a fuel joins with oxygen very fast and gives out heat and light. It makes new substances. These new substances are called the products.
explanations.description: Melting wax is a change of state. The wax stays wax. Burning wax is different, because new substances appear. The wax gas joins with oxygen from the air. The atoms of the wax and the atoms of the oxygen come apart and join up again in a new way, and that makes carbon dioxide and water. Scientists call a change like this a chemical reaction. You can tell a chemical reaction has happened when the starting things cannot be got back easily, when new things appear, and when heat or light is given out. Burning shows all three. You cannot turn ash and smoke back into a log.
examples: Wax burning makes carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Cooking gas burning makes the same two things.
Rusting is also a reaction with oxygen, only very slow.
explanations.art: Wax atoms and oxygen atoms on the left, drawn as coloured balls, rearranging into carbon dioxide and water on the right, with a flame between them.

explanations.concept: What a flame makes: water, carbon dioxide and soot
explanations.definition: A candle flame makes water vapour and carbon dioxide, which are invisible, and a little soot, which is black. The cold plate in the first activity catches the water and the soot.
explanations.description: Wax is made of two kinds of atoms, carbon and hydrogen, joined in long chains. When the wax gas burns, the carbon joins with oxygen to make carbon dioxide. The hydrogen joins with oxygen to make water, which is a hot gas inside the flame. Both gases are invisible, and they rise up and mix into the air. When water vapour touches a cold plate, it cools and turns back into drops. That is the wet patch you saw. The black patch is soot. In a yellow flame, some of the carbon is not burnt, and it comes out as tiny black bits. A candle never vanishes. It turns into things that are spread through the air of the room.
examples: Drops on a cold plate over a flame are water that the flame made.
Black soot on a spoon held in a flame is unburnt carbon.
The carbon dioxide from a flame is invisible, but it is in the air above it.
explanations.art: A candle flame with a cold plate above it, and arrows showing water drops and soot collecting, and an invisible gas drifting up and spreading out.

explanations.concept: Nothing is lost: burning swaps partners
explanations.definition: In every chemical reaction the total mass stays the same. The atoms that were there at the start are all still there at the end. They have only changed partners.
explanations.description: When a log burns, it seems to shrink to a little ash. But the log was also joining with oxygen from the air, and most of what it became was gas that floated away. If a log and all the oxygen it used could be weighed, and then all the gas and ash it made, the two weights would match. Steel wool shows this clearly. Iron is not a gas, so when it burns it joins with oxygen and becomes a solid iron oxide. The burnt steel wool is heavier, because it holds the oxygen it took from the air. The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier showed in the 1770s and 1780s that weighing everything, including the gases, gives the same total. Physicists later found that heat leaving a fire carries away a tiny amount of mass, about a fifth of a millionth of a gram for every kilogram of wood. So 'nothing is lost' is true to better than one part in a billion.
examples: Burning steel wool gets heavier, because it takes oxygen from the air.
A log leaves little ash, because most of it became gas that floats away.
A sealed jar with a burning candle weighs the same before and after.
explanations.art: A balance with a log and a jar of air on one side and ash, water and carbon dioxide in jars on the other side, both pans level.

explanations.concept: How fast something burns depends on how fast oxygen reaches it
explanations.definition: A fuel burns only where oxygen can touch it. The more surface a fuel shows to the air, and the faster fresh air arrives, the faster it burns.
explanations.description: Oxygen has to reach the fuel's surface, or the fuel's gas, for burning to go on. A log lying in the fire burns slowly, because only its outside meets the air. A pile of thin twigs burns fast, because every twig shows a lot of surface. That is why people split wood into kindling before they build a fire, and why they blow on embers. Blowing sends in fresh air, which brings new oxygen. A tightly rolled newspaper may even go out part-way, because the middle gets too little air. Flour is not something that seems to burn, but a cloud of flour dust in the air has so much surface that it can burn in a flash. Mills and grain stores have been wrecked by this, so they keep dust and sparks away.
examples: Thin kindling lights faster than a thick log.
Blowing on embers makes them glow brighter, because it brings in oxygen.
Flour dust in a mill burns far faster than a heap of flour.
explanations.art: A thick log and a pile of thin twigs on a fire, with arrows of air reaching many more places on the twigs.

explanations.concept: Complete and incomplete burning: blue flames and yellow flames
explanations.definition: With plenty of oxygen, fuel burns completely, and the flame is blue. With too little oxygen, fuel burns incompletely, and the flame is yellow, makes soot, and can make carbon monoxide.
explanations.description: A gas stove has small air holes at the base of each burner. They let air mix with the gas before it burns, so there is plenty of oxygen. The carbon burns completely to carbon dioxide, and the flame is blue and makes no soot. A candle flame is different. Wax gas rises in the middle with little air, so some carbon is left over as tiny bits of soot. Inside the flame, the soot is very hot, and it glows yellow, just as a heated iron rod glows red. When burning is incomplete, a second product can form. Carbon monoxide is a gas with no colour and no smell, and it is poisonous because it stops the blood carrying oxygen. That is why a coal or charcoal fire must never burn in a closed room. A stove whose flame turns yellow and blackens the pans needs cleaning.
examples: A clean gas stove burns blue, and a smoky chulha burns yellow.
A pan that turns black on the bottom shows soot from incomplete burning.
A coal fire in a shut room can make carbon monoxide.
explanations.art: A blue stove flame with air arrows at the base next to a yellow candle flame with black soot specks glowing in the middle.

explanations.concept: Where the heat and light come from: old sunlight, and your own breath
explanations.definition: A fuel stores energy in the way its atoms are joined. When the atoms rearrange into carbon dioxide and water, they are held together more tightly, and the extra energy is given out as heat and light.
explanations.description: Plants build wood, oil and sugar from carbon dioxide and water, using the energy of sunlight. That energy is stored in the way the atoms are joined. When the fuel burns, the atoms rearrange and give the energy back as heat and light. So a fire is sunlight that a plant stored, set free again. Coal and petrol are stored sunlight from plants and tiny sea animals that lived millions of years ago. Your body does a slow version of the same thing. Cells combine sugar from your food with oxygen from your breath, and make carbon dioxide and water, just like a candle. But they do it slowly, in many small steps, so the energy comes out as body warmth and movement, not as a flame. Breathe on a cold plate, and you will see the same fog that a flame makes.
examples: Burning wood gives back sunlight that the tree stored.
Petrol and coal are old plants and tiny animals, burnt millions of years later.
Breathing makes carbon dioxide and water, as burning does.
explanations.art: A sun, a tree, a log on a fire and a child breathing out, joined by arrows that show the same energy passing along.

explanations.concept: A flame's colour tells which atoms are burning
explanations.definition: Atoms of each element give out light of their own colours when they are heated in a flame. So the colour of a flame can show which element is burning.
explanations.description: Sprinkle a pinch of salt in a gas flame, and it flashes a bright yellow-orange. The salt contains sodium. Atoms of sodium, when heated, give out yellow light, and nothing else. Copper gives green, and strontium gives red, which is why fireworks have their colours. Each element has its own colours, like a fingerprint. In 1868, a French astronomer called Pierre Janssen watched a total eclipse of the Sun from Guntur in India. He split the light from the edge of the Sun and saw a bright yellow line that did not match any known element. The British astronomer Norman Lockyer saw the same line and named the new element helium, after the Greek word for the Sun. It was found on Earth in 1895. Later, Cecilia Payne used the same method to show that the Sun is made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
examples: A pinch of salt turns a flame yellow-orange, because of sodium.
Fireworks use different metals to make red, green and blue.
Light from a star shows which elements are in it.
explanations.art: Four flames in a row coloured yellow, green, red and blue, each labelled with a metal, and a spectrum band below.

explanations.concept: Carbon dioxide puts fires out, and water can make some fires worse
explanations.definition: A fire can be put out by cutting off its oxygen, taking away its heat, or removing its fuel. Carbon dioxide and a lid cut off oxygen. Water takes away heat, but it spreads a burning oil fire instead of stopping it.
explanations.description: Carbon dioxide does not burn, and it is heavier than air. So it can be poured over a flame like water, and it pushes the air, and the oxygen, away from the fuel. Some fire extinguishers hold carbon dioxide for this reason. Water works on a wood fire because it cools the fuel. But oil floats on water. If water is thrown onto a burning pan of oil, the water sinks beneath the oil and turns to steam in a second, and the steam throws burning oil in all directions. So a burning pan is covered with a lid or a damp cloth to shut out oxygen. Water must also never be used on an electrical fire, because water conducts electricity.
examples: A lid on a burning pan cuts off its air.
A carbon dioxide extinguisher pours out a heavy gas that covers the fire.
Water cools a burning wood fire.
explanations.art: A child tilting a jar to pour an invisible gas over a candle flame in a bowl, and the flame going out, with a lid on a pan beside them.

explanations.definition: The Sun does not burn. Burning needs oxygen, and the Sun has almost none. The Sun shines by fusion, in which hydrogen joins together to make helium deep in its centre.
explanations.description: If the Sun were a giant ball of coal burning in oxygen, it would have run out of fuel in about five thousand years. But the Sun has been shining for about four and a half billion years. Fusion gives far more energy from each gram than burning does. In the Sun's centre it is so hot and squeezed that the centres of hydrogen atoms are pushed together and join to make helium. Each time, a tiny bit of mass turns into a huge amount of energy. This is the E equals m c squared idea. So the Sun is not a fire, but it is the source of nearly all the energy in the fires on Earth. Plants stored its light in wood, oil and coal.
examples: The Sun has no oxygen to burn in.
A coal Sun would have run out in about five thousand years.
Nearly all the fuel on Earth is stored sunlight.
explanations.art: The Sun with a cut-away showing hydrogen atoms joining into helium in the centre, and a small candle beside it for comparison.

explanations.concept: Fire in space: flames that are round and blue
explanations.description: On Earth a flame points up, because hot gas is lighter than cool air and rises, and pulls fresh air in from below. In the weightlessness of the International Space Station, hot gas does not rise. Astronauts' experiments have shown that a candle flame there is a small, round, blue ball. It gets oxygen only by slow drifting, so it burns weakly and soot barely forms. Over some years, scientists on the station found something odd, and reported it in 2014. Tiny drops of fuel kept burning after the visible flame had gone out. They burned at a much lower temperature, in an invisible 'cool flame'. Scientists are still studying how these cool flames work, because they may help make cleaner engines.
examples: A candle flame on the space station is round and blue.
Weightless hot gas does not rise.
Cool flames burn fuel without a visible flame.
explanations.art: An astronaut inside a space station looking at a small round blue flame floating in the air, next to an Earth candle with a teardrop flame.

explanations.concept: What is a flame made of?
explanations.description: A flame is not a solid, a liquid or a plain gas. It is a glowing place where fuel gas and oxygen are joining. Scientists agree on that, but they disagree on what to call the stuff inside it. Some of the atoms in a flame lose electrons, and this makes a very small share of the flame electrically charged. You can bend a flame with a charged rod.
examples: A flame glows because of hot soot and excited molecules.
A flame can be bent a little by a charged object.
A flame is a place where a reaction happens, not a thing you can hold.
explanations.art: A candle flame drawn with a magnified circle showing a few charged particles among many ordinary molecules.

perspectives.explanation: A flame is a hot, glowing gas where a reaction is going on. Only a tiny share of it is charged, so calling it a plasma tells us little.
Any gas with charged particles that respond to electric fields is a plasma. A flame has them, so it counts as a weakly charged plasma, although a very cool one.

agreed.text: Burning is a chemical reaction in which a fuel joins with oxygen. It gives out heat and light.
agreed.evidence: Weighing the fuel, the oxygen used and the products, as Lavoisier did, gives the same total. Carbon dioxide and water are found in the products of a candle.

agreed.text: In a chemical reaction, the total mass stays the same.
agreed.evidence: Chemists have weighed sealed flasks before and after thousands of reactions since the 1770s, and the weight does not change.

agreed.text: A candle flame makes water vapour, carbon dioxide and soot.
agreed.evidence: A cold plate over a flame collects drops of water and black soot. Carbon dioxide can be shown with limewater, which turns milky.

agreed.text: Fire needs fuel, oxygen and enough heat. Take away any one, and it goes out.
agreed.evidence: Every fire extinguisher works by removing one of the three.

agreed.text: The Sun shines by fusion, not by burning.
agreed.evidence: Burning could power the Sun for only a few thousand years. Rocks, meteorites and radioactive dating show that the Sun is billions of years old.

agreed.text: Atoms of each element give out their own colours of light when heated.
agreed.evidence: Salt always makes a flame yellow, and copper always makes it green. Starlight shows the same colours, so astronomers can tell what stars are made of.

challenging.claim: When something burns, it is destroyed.
challenging.who: Many people, and many young children.
challenging.for: A log really does turn into a pinch of ash, and a candle gets shorter until it is gone.
challenging.against: The missing part has become invisible gases and soot. Weighed with the oxygen it used, a burnt thing has the same total mass.

challenging.claim: Burning things give off phlogiston, and that is why they burn.
challenging.who: Georg Stahl and many chemists of the 1700s.
challenging.for: Wood and coal are left as light ash, as if something had escaped. The idea explained many things.
challenging.against: When tin or iron burns, it gets heavier. Lavoisier showed that it takes something from the air, which he named oxygen.

challenging.claim: A candle goes out in a closed jar because all the oxygen is used up.
challenging.for: The flame does go out in a closed jar, and it does need oxygen.
challenging.against: Air has about 21 parts oxygen in every 100. A candle goes out while much of the oxygen is still left in the air. The carbon dioxide and heat also matter.

challenging.claim: The Sun is a giant ball of fire.
challenging.for: The Sun gives heat and light, and looks like a flame.
challenging.against: There is almost no oxygen in space, and burning could not last more than a few thousand years. The Sun runs on fusion.

challenging.claim: Fire is a basic element of the world, not a process.
challenging.who: The Greek thinkers who named four elements, and Indian traditions that list five great elements, including fire, or agni.
challenging.for: Fire looks like something with a nature of its own: it rises, it glows, and it changes everything it touches.
challenging.against: In chemistry a flame is a reaction between a fuel and oxygen, and it stops when either is gone. In the old traditions, fire also stood for the power of heat and change, which is not the same claim.

big_questions.q: A log leaves almost no ash, but burning steel wool gets heavier. Where does the log go, and where does the extra weight on the steel wool come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about which of the products are gases, and which are solid.

big_questions.q: If nothing is ever lost when something burns, what do we mean when we say a candle is gone?
big_questions.hint: Think about the difference between the atoms and the candle as a candle.

big_questions.q: Is the flame glowing, or are the tiny bits of soot inside the flame glowing?
big_questions.hint: Think about the hot iron rod that glows red, and about the blue part of a flame that has no soot.

big_questions.q: Rusting and burning both join a material with oxygen, but one takes years and the other a few seconds. Is it the same change?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is the same in the two changes, and what is different.

big_questions.q: Your breath fogs a cold plate in the same way a flame does. What does this tell us about how a living body gets its energy?
big_questions.hint: Think about food, oxygen, and what comes out of your mouth.

big_questions.q: A snake feels the heat of a flame, and we see the flame's light. Are we seeing the same flame differently, or are we meeting different things?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each body can sense, and what 'the flame' would be without any body to meet it.

big_questions.q: A cooking fire gives a family food, but the smoke harms the people who stand near it, mostly women and children. How should we weigh a gain and a harm that come from the same thing?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets the benefit, who gets the harm, and what might make a fire cleaner.

big_questions.q: Wood is old sunlight that a tree stored. When we burn wood, whose sunlight are we spending?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long the energy waited, and how fast we use it.

story.title: The Weight of the Ash
story.note: The story is made up. Bhogi is a real festival on the morning before Pongal, when families burn old things, and in some cities the smoke from burnt plastic and tyres is a real problem. Everything in the story about what burning makes is true. A hundred and twenty grams of ash from three kilograms of dry fronds is a believable amount.
text: On the morning before Pongal, a village near Madurai was awake long before the sun. It was Bhogi. All along the lane, families were piling up old things to burn. There were broken stools, torn mats and bundles of dry coconut fronds. Thamarai was nine, and she had been up since four. She stood next to her grandfather, Thatha, in front of their house.
Thatha rubbed his hands in the cold. "This is the best day of the year for letting go," he said. "Fire takes the old away. By morning it is gone for ever, and we start new."

Thamarai looked at the pile. The night before, she had borrowed the grocer's beam balance, the tharasu, with its two steel pans. She had weighed the bundle of fronds. It had been three kilograms exactly. "Thatha," she said, "tomorrow I want to weigh what is left. Then we will know how much has gone."
Thatha laughed. "All of it will have gone, kanna."

Just then her cousin Ravi came running down the lane. He was pulling an old scooter tyre behind him. After him came Aunty Selvi, carrying a basket of cracked plastic buckets and a torn plastic mat. "Put them on the pile," said Thatha. "They are old too."

Thamarai frowned. She remembered last year. The black smoke from the tyre had hung over the lane for hours. The baby next door, Anbu, had coughed all night. "Wait," she said. "Before we light it, I want to show you something."

She ran inside and came back with a steel tumbler of cold water and a candle stub. Paati came out behind her, wiping her hands on her sari. Thamarai lit the candle on a flat stone. "Watch the bottom of the tumbler," she said. She held it high above the flame, and then lower.
At first nothing happened. Then the outside of the tumbler turned misty. Tiny drops joined together and began to run. Thatha leaned closer. "Water?" he said. "But a candle is wax. It is not water."

"Look lower," said Thamarai. She moved the tumbler right into the yellow tip of the flame. When she lifted it, a black patch had appeared on the steel. Paati touched it, and her finger came away black.

"The wax did not vanish," said Thamarai. "The flame made it into water and into a gas we cannot see. They went up into the air. The black is the part that did not burn properly. It is called soot." She stood up straight. "So when I weigh the ash tomorrow, it will be tiny. But the fronds will not be gone. They will be in the air."
Nobody said anything for a moment. A crow shouted from the roof. Then Thatha said slowly, "If the fronds go into the air, then the tyre goes into the air as well."
"Yes, Thatha," said Thamarai. "And it makes black smoke, and we breathe it. Anbu breathes it."

Thatha looked at the tyre, and then at the house next door, where a small light was on. He took a long breath. "I have been burning old things for sixty years," he said. "I thought I was getting rid of them." He turned. "Ravi, Selvi, take the tyre and the plastic out of the pile. The panchayat cart comes on Saturday. Let them take it away."
"But it will still be old, Thatha," said Ravi.
"It will be old," said Thamarai. "But it will be somewhere we choose, and not in the lane."

Thatha struck a match. The dry fronds caught at once. Orange flames leaned up into the dark, and the whole lane glowed. The smoke that rose was thin and pale. Paati put the new Pongal pot on three stones, and the village began to sing.

When the fire had burned down, Thamarai knelt and scooped the grey ash into the steel pan of the tharasu. She put the weight on the other pan. It came to one hundred and twenty grams. She wrote it down. Three thousand grams had gone into the fire, and one hundred and twenty had come out.
"Where did the rest go?" Ravi asked.

Thamarai pointed up at the sky, which was turning pink above the smoke. "Up there," she said. "Water, and the same gas that you breathe out. And a little of the sunlight that the palm tree stored while growing."
Thatha put a hand on her head. "Then I have a lot to learn about letting go," he said. "It seems nothing ever really goes away. It only goes somewhere else."
story.epiphany: Burning does not make things vanish. Wood, wax and plastic all turn into gases and ash, so everything we burn goes into the air around us.

Why is burning a tyre not the same as getting rid of it?

games.context: In this game, each card describes a change. You decide if it is fast burning, slow joining with oxygen, or a change that makes no new substance, and say why.

items.f: A candle burns on a table.
items.b: Fast burning. The wax gas joins with oxygen fast, and gives out heat and light.

items.f: An iron nail rusts in a damp corner over a year.
items.b: Slow joining with oxygen. Iron joins with oxygen slowly and becomes rust.

items.f: Wax melts in a warm diya.
items.b: No new substance. Melting only changes the state. The wax is still wax.

items.f: A cut apple turns brown on a plate.
items.b: Slow joining with oxygen. Substances in the apple join with oxygen from the air, slowly.

items.f: Water boils in a pan.
items.b: No new substance. The water becomes steam, which is still water.

items.f: You run, and your cells use food and oxygen to make energy.
items.b: Slow joining with oxygen. Respiration makes carbon dioxide and water, as burning does, but slowly and in small steps.

items.f: A gas stove burns LPG under a pan.
items.b: Fast burning. LPG joins with oxygen and gives out heat and light.

items.f: A wet cloth dries in the sun.
items.b: No new substance. The water becomes vapour and leaves the cloth. It is still water.

items.f: A sparkler spits white sparks.
items.b: Fast burning. Tiny bits of metal burn very fast in the air.

items.f: A tuft of steel wool glows and turns grey.
items.b: Fast burning. Iron joins with oxygen and becomes iron oxide, which is heavier.

items.f: A banana peel turns black and soft in a bin.
items.b: Slow joining with oxygen. Tiny living beings break it down, and use oxygen as they do.

items.f: An ice cube melts in a glass.
items.b: No new substance. Ice is only water in its solid state.

items.f: An electric heater's wire glows red.
items.b: No new substance. Electricity heats the wire so that it glows, but the wire is not burning.

items.f: A torch bulb glows white.
items.b: No new substance. The thin wire inside glows because it is hot. The bulb has no oxygen to burn in.

items.f: Sugar dissolves in a glass of tea.
items.b: No new substance. The sugar mixes with the water. It is still sugar.

items.f: Camphor burns on an arati plate and leaves nothing behind.
items.b: Fast burning. Camphor joins with oxygen and becomes invisible gases.

items.f: A bicycle chain left in the rain turns orange-brown.
items.b: Slow joining with oxygen. The iron slowly becomes rust.

items.f: Dry wood in a chulha glows red and becomes ash.
items.b: Fast burning. Wood joins with oxygen, and gives out heat and light.

items.f: Salt dissolves in a bowl of water.
items.b: No new substance. The salt is only spread out in the water. It is still salt.

items.f: A copper pot turns dark and dull over many months.
items.b: Slow joining with oxygen. Copper slowly joins with oxygen from the air, and makes a dark layer.

printables.title: 12 tokens: four of each kind, 'Fast burning', 'Slow joining with oxygen' and 'No new substance'

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Then everyone turns their token over together.
The reader reads the back. Every player whose token matches the first words of the back scores one point.
A player who also says why in one sentence, using the words oxygen, new or air correctly, scores one more point. The reader decides, using the back of the card.
After each card, the job of reader passes to the player on the left. With two players, swap after every card.

Playing alone: read the front, say your answer and your reason out loud, then turn the card over. Score one point for each correct answer and one for each good reason. Try to beat your best score out of 40.
The game ends when all 20 cards have been read. The player with most points wins. If there is a tie, the tied players share the win.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile. Give each player a set of three tokens. Read the three kinds aloud, and explain each one with the examples from the first three cards.
flow.say: There are three kinds of change. Fast burning joins with oxygen and gives heat and light. Slow joining is the same thing, but slow. In the third kind, nothing new is made.
flow.kid: Three kinds: fast burning, slow joining with oxygen, and no new substance.

ask.q: Which kind of change do you think rusting is?

flow.parent: Let your child read the tokens aloud. The key idea is that a new substance means a chemical change. Melting, dissolving and boiling are not chemical changes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fast, Slow or Not New. You learn the three kinds and set up.

flow.do: Play the first eight cards. After each card, read the back aloud. After card four, ask the question below.
flow.say: The reader reads the front. Everyone picks a token. Turn them over together. The reader reads the back. Who scored a point? Who can say why?
flow.kid: The reader reads a card. Pick a token. Turn it over. Check the back.

ask.q: What do the fast burning and slow joining cards have in common?

flow.parent: Do not let the reader show the back before everyone has chosen. If your child has not heard of an item, let them guess from the clue in the card.
flow.context: In this step, you play the first eight cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the last twelve cards. At the end, count the points. Ask the final question below.
flow.say: Keep going until all the cards are read. Count your points. Who has the most? Then tell me which cards were the trickiest.
flow.kid: Finish the cards. Count your points. Which card was trickiest?

ask.q: A heater wire glows red, but it is not burning. How can something glow without burning?
good: It is hot, so it gives out light.

flow.parent: The trickiest cards are usually the heater wire and the torch bulb. Things glow when they are hot enough, whether or not they burn.

check.q: A card says: 'A copper pot turns dark over many months.' Which kind of change is it?
check.why: The dark layer is a new substance made when copper joins slowly with oxygen. It takes months, so it is the slow kind. It has no flame, so it is not the fast kind.

flow.context: In this step, you finish the cards and count the points.

experiments.title: Same Paper, Three Shapes: which burns fastest?
experiments.question: A sheet of newspaper can be left flat, crumpled loosely or rolled tightly. Which shape burns fastest, and which burns slowest?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which shape will burn fastest, and which will burn slowest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every piece is cut from the same newspaper and is exactly 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres, so it has the same weight. The adult lights each piece at its bottom edge with a match, in the same place, in a room with no fan. The timer starts when the paper catches fire, and stops when the last flame goes out. Only the shape changes, so any difference comes from the shape. Each shape is tested twice.
results_table: Did the middle go out and stay unburnt?

materials.item: 6 pieces of old newspaper, each exactly 20 centimetres by 20 centimetres
a ruler and a pair of scissors
a pencil to roll one piece round
a pair of metal kitchen tongs, a long matchbox or a lighter, for the grown-up only
an empty steel kitchen sink or a big steel tray, to burn the paper over
a bucket of water and a damp cloth, close by
a phone or clock with a stopwatch, and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights and holds every piece. Burn the paper over the steel sink or tray, away from curtains, with a bucket of water beside you. Tie back long hair and loose sleeves. Open a window.
experiments.record: Write the time for each try and whether any paper stayed unburnt. Then draw a bar chart with one bar for each shape, using the average of the two tries.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you burn the same newspaper in three shapes and time how long each takes. You find out what changes the speed of burning.

setup.art: Three pieces of newspaper on a table: one flat, one crumpled loosely into a ball, and one rolled tightly round a pencil.
setup.caption: 1. Make three shapes from three equal pieces: flat, a loose ball, and a tight roll.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the top of a flat sheet with kitchen tongs over a steel sink, and lighting the bottom edge with a match.
setup.caption: 2. The grown-up holds one piece with tongs over the sink and lights its bottom.

setup.art: A child holding a phone stopwatch, watching the burning paper closely.
setup.caption: 3. Start the timer when it catches, and stop it when the last flame is out.

setup.art: A results table with three rows and a pencil, and three bars drawn next to it.
setup.caption: 4. Write each time in the table. Repeat, then draw a bar for each shape.

flow.do: Show your child the three shapes. Ask for a guess about which burns fastest and slowest. Write down their reason.
flow.say: The three shapes are made of exactly the same paper. Which one will burn fastest? Which will burn slowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Same paper in three shapes. Which burns fastest? Which burns slowest? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that shape will burn fastest?
good: It has more air around it.
It is packed tight, so it burns slowly.
The flame can reach more of it.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write the guesses at the top of the table.
flow.context: This is the first step of the paper test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Cut six pieces of newspaper, each 20 centimetres square. Leave two flat. Crumple two loosely into balls. Roll two tightly round a pencil, and slide the pencil out.
flow.say: Measure each piece with the ruler. Make them all the same size. Two stay flat, two become loose balls, and two become tight rolls.
flow.kid: Cut six equal squares of newspaper. Leave two flat. Crumple two. Roll two tight.
flow.parent: Use the same newspaper page for all six, so the paper is the same thickness. Keep them away from the burning area until it is their turn.

check.q: Why must all the pieces be cut to the same size?
options: So the paper does not tear
check.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. If one piece were bigger, you would not know if the size or the shape made the difference.

flow.context: In this step, you cut and shape the six pieces of paper.

flow.do: Set the sink or tray ready, with the water beside it. Hold the first flat piece at its top with the tongs, over the sink. Light its bottom edge. Your child starts the timer when it catches and stops it when the last flame is out.
flow.say: I hold the paper over the sink and light the bottom. When it catches, you press start. When the last flame is out, you press stop. Read me the time.
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the paper. You time it. Start when it catches. Stop when it is out.

ask.q: What do you see the flame doing as it moves along the paper?
good: It moves where there is more paper to burn.

flow.parent: The flat piece may burn in only a few seconds. Count a few more seconds to be sure the glow has gone. If a piece drops, let it burn out in the sink. Never lean over the flame.
flow.context: In this step, the grown-up burns the flat piece while your child times it.

flow.do: Burn the loose ball and the tight roll in the same way, one at a time. Burn the second flat piece, the second ball and the second roll. Write each time. Note if any middle stayed unburnt.
flow.say: Now the loose ball, and then the tight roll. Time each one. Look at the middle of the roll when it is done. Is any paper left?
flow.kid: Time the ball. Time the roll. Look at the middle. Is any paper left?

ask.q: What is different about how the roll burns, compared with the flat sheet?

flow.parent: The tight roll may burn slowly, or go out part-way. If it goes out, write 'went out' in the last column and stop the timer at that moment. That is a result too. Times will vary a little between tries.

check.q: Why do we burn each shape twice?
options: One try can be a fluke
check.why: A single try might be odd, because of a draught or the way the match lit it. Two close results show the test gives about the same answer each time.

flow.context: In this step, the other shapes are burned, and you time and write down each try.

flow.do: Draw a bar chart with one bar for each shape, using the average of the two tries. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Draw a bar for each shape. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: Why did the shapes made of the same paper burn at different speeds?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the flame needs air to reach the paper, and the more of the paper is open to the air, the faster it burns. The tight roll has little air inside it. After they have said what they saw, explain: burning goes only where oxygen touches the fuel. Many families find the roll slowest and the others faster, but yours may differ.
flow.context: This is the last step of the paper test. You draw the chart and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Lighter or Heavier? Burning steel wool on a homemade balance
experiments.question: Two equal tufts of steel wool hang from the ends of a balance. If a grown-up burns one of them, will that side go up, go down, or stay level?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. When one tuft burns, will its side of the balance go up, go down or stay level? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both tufts are pulled from the same pad of steel wool and hung the same distance from the middle. The balance is level before anything is lit. Only one tuft is burned, and the other is the control. Any change in the balance comes from the burning.
results_table: Is the balance level, or which side is lower?
What does the burned tuft look like?

materials.item: fine steel wool, the iron kind from a hardware shop, grade 0 or finer (a stainless steel kitchen scrubber will not work)
a wooden skewer or thin stick about 30 centimetres long
thread, two paper clips, and a pencil or ruler to hang the balance from
a small ball of modelling clay or sticky tape, for fine balancing
a steel tray or thali to catch sparks, and a bowl of water
matches or a lighter, for the grown-up only
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up lights the steel wool. It glows and throws tiny sparks. Work over a steel tray, away from curtains and paper, with a bowl of water close by. Do not touch the burnt wool until it has cooled for ten minutes.
experiments.record: In the table, write what the balance did before burning, during burning and after cooling. Draw the balance in all three moments.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you burn steel wool on one side of a homemade balance. You find out whether burning makes it lighter or heavier.

setup.art: A wooden skewer hung from its middle by a thread tied to a pencil taped to a shelf edge, hanging level.
setup.caption: 1. Hang the skewer from its middle on a thread. Slide the thread until it hangs level.

setup.art: Two equal tufts of steel wool, each hooked on a paper clip, hanging from the two ends of the skewer, which hangs level.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a tuft of steel wool of equal size from each end. Adjust until the balance is level.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a match to one tuft over a steel tray, with the tuft glowing orange and small sparks falling.
setup.caption: 3. The grown-up lights one tuft. It glows and burns.

setup.art: The skewer tilted with the burnt tuft lower and the unburnt tuft higher, over the steel tray.
setup.caption: 4. When it has cooled, look at the balance. Which side is lower?

flow.do: Show your child the steel wool. Say that one tuft will be burned. Ask for a guess about the balance, and the reason. Write it down.
flow.say: When this steel wool burns, it will turn grey and crumbly. Will its side of the balance go up, go down, or stay level? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One tuft will burn. Will its side go up, go down or stay level? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think it will go up?
good: The fire eats it, so it gets lighter.

flow.parent: Most families guess it will go up, because burning seems to use things up. Do not correct the guess. Write it down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the steel wool test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Tie a thread round the middle of the skewer. Tie its other end to a pencil taped to a shelf edge. Slide the thread until the skewer hangs level. Hook two paper clips at the ends, the same distance from the middle.
flow.say: The thread goes round the middle of the stick. Slide it until the stick hangs flat. Then hang one paper clip at each end, the same distance from the middle.
flow.kid: Hang the stick from its middle. Make it level. Hang a clip at each end.
flow.parent: Make this balance first, without the steel wool. It will swing and wobble. Wait until it is still. Tape or clay a tiny weight to the higher end if it will not level.

check.q: Why must the balance hang level before anything is burned?
options: So we can tell if burning changed it
So the thread does not slip
check.why: A level balance is the starting line. If it were tilted already, you could not tell whether burning changed anything.

flow.context: In this step, you build the balance from a stick and a thread.

flow.do: Pull two tufts from the steel wool, each about the size of a walnut. Fluff each one gently. Push one onto each paper clip. Adjust the tufts until the balance is level again.
flow.say: Pull out two tufts of steel wool, the same size. Fluff them up. Hang one on each clip. Is the balance level? If not, pinch a bit off the heavier one.
flow.kid: Make two equal tufts. Hang one on each side. Make the balance level.
flow.parent: Wash your hands after touching steel wool, because tiny slivers can prick. Keep the tufts loose and fluffy, which helps them burn. Place the steel tray under the balance now.
flow.context: In this step, you hang two equal tufts of steel wool so the balance is level.

flow.do: Clear everything flammable from around the balance. The grown-up holds a lit match to the tip of one tuft until it starts to glow. Then step back. Watch it glow and spread for a few minutes. Let it cool for ten minutes.
flow.say: I light one tuft, and then we step back. Watch it glow. See how the glow spreads. What is happening to the balance while it burns?
flow.kid: A grown-up lights one tuft. Watch it glow. Stay back. Watch the balance.

ask.q: What do you see happening to the steel wool as it burns?

flow.parent: If the tuft only glows a little and stops, light it again at another spot. If it does not burn at all, it is probably stainless steel wool, which will not work. A few sparks may drop. The tray will catch them. Wait until it is cold before you touch it.
flow.context: In this step, the grown-up burns one tuft, and you watch what happens.

flow.do: When the burnt tuft is cold, look at the balance. Which side is lower? Draw it. Then ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Which side is lower? Draw it. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.think: The steel wool burned, so why did its side get heavier?
flow.parent: In most tries, the burnt side goes down. It is a big surprise. After they have said what they saw, explain: iron is a solid, so nothing floats away. As it burns, it joins with oxygen from the air and becomes a solid iron oxide. The extra weight is oxygen. If the balance did not tilt, little of the wool burned, so try again with a looser tuft.

check.q: The burnt steel wool is heavier. Where did the extra weight come from?
options: Oxygen from the air that joined with the iron
check.why: Burning iron joins with oxygen from the air and makes a solid. That solid weighs as much as the iron plus the oxygen. The weight was in the air all along, but we could not see it.

flow.context: This is the last step of the steel wool test. You look at the balance and explain what you found.

activities.title: Catch What a Flame Makes: water and soot from a candle

materials.item: a tea-light candle in its metal cup, standing on a steel plate or thali
two identical steel katoris or small steel bowls
ice cubes and cold water
a steel spoon
a cloth to dry the katoris, and matches for the grown-up
a cold steel plate or a mirror, for the breath test
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Guess. Hold a cold katori over the flame, and another beside it. Catch soot on a spoon. Breathe on a cold plate. Compare.

activities.safety: A grown-up lights the candle and holds the katori and spoon over it. Tie back long hair and loose sleeves. Keep the candle away from curtains and paper. The spoon and the katori's underside get hot or sooty, so do not touch them for a minute.
activities.record: Draw the two katoris after the test, and the spoon. Write what each one caught, and where you think it came from.
activities.context: In this activity, you hold a cold katori over a flame and see what the flame leaves behind. You also compare it with your own breath.

setup.art: Two steel katoris filled with ice water, wiped dry on the outside, one held above a candle flame and one held beside it at the same height.
setup.caption: 1. Fill two katoris with ice water and wipe them dry. Hold one above the flame and one beside it.

setup.art: The underside of the katori held above the flame, covered in drops of water, next to the other katori which is almost dry.
setup.caption: 2. After 20 seconds, compare the outsides of the two katoris.

setup.art: A steel spoon held for two seconds in the yellow tip of a candle flame, and then showing a black patch.
setup.caption: 3. Hold the spoon in the yellow part of the flame for two seconds. Look at the black patch.

setup.art: A child breathing out onto a cold steel plate, which has a patch of fog on it.
setup.caption: 4. Breathe onto a cold plate. Compare its fog with the katori's drops.

flow.do: Show your child the candle and the cold katori. Ask what they think will happen to the katori when held above the flame. Write down their guess and the reason.
flow.say: We will hold a cold bowl above a flame. What do you think we will find on the bowl? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A cold bowl will be held above a flame. What will you find on it? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think anything on the bowl will come from?

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. Some children will say that nothing happens, and that is fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of Catch What a Flame Makes. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Fill both katoris with ice water. Wipe the outsides dry. Light the tea-light. Hold one katori 3 centimetres above the flame tip. Hold the other at the same height beside the flame. Count to 20.
flow.say: Two cold bowls, wiped dry. One goes over the flame. The other stays beside it. We count to twenty. Now look at the outsides of both.
flow.kid: Hold one cold bowl over the flame. Hold one beside it. Count to 20. Look at both.

ask.q: How are the two katoris different? Why would they be different?
good: The one over the flame is wetter.
The one beside the flame is nearly dry.

flow.parent: On a humid day, the bowl beside the flame will fog a little too, because cold steel makes water out of the room air. That is why we have two bowls. The bowl over the flame should be clearly wetter, with big drops that run. If both look the same, hold the first bowl lower, and count to 30.

check.q: Why do we hold a second cold bowl beside the flame?
options: To see if the drops come from the room air and not the flame
To keep the first bowl company
check.why: A cold bowl can collect water from the room's air even without a flame. The second bowl shows how much of that to expect. Only the extra water on the first bowl comes from the flame.

flow.context: In this step, you hold a cold katori over the flame and one beside it, and compare them.

flow.do: Hold the steel spoon in the yellow tip of the flame for two seconds. Take it out. Look at the underside. Rub the black patch with a wet finger.
flow.say: Now the spoon, in the yellow tip, for two seconds. Look at the black patch. Rub it with a wet finger. What is it? Where did it come from?
flow.kid: A grown-up holds the spoon in the flame for two seconds. Look at the black patch. What is it?

ask.q: What do you think the black patch is made of?

flow.parent: The black patch is soot, which is carbon from the wax that did not burn completely. If the spoon is clean, hold it in the yellow tip a little longer, but not in the blue base.
flow.context: In this step, you catch black soot from the yellow part of the flame.

flow.do: Breathe out slowly onto a cold steel plate, as you would onto a mirror. Look at the fog. Compare it with the drops on the katori from the flame.
flow.say: Breathe out slowly onto the cold plate. What do you see? How is it like what the flame made?
flow.kid: Breathe on the cold plate. What do you see? Is it like the flame's drops?

ask.q: Why do you think your breath and the flame make the same thing?

flow.parent: Your breath is full of water vapour and carbon dioxide, just as a flame is. Your body breaks down food with oxygen, slowly. You do not need to explain this yet, only to notice that the two fogs look alike.
flow.context: In this step, you compare your breath with what the flame made.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. Then draw the katoris and the spoon.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Draw the bowls and the spoon.
flow.think: The candle is wax. How can a flame make water?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the candle made water and soot, so the wax changed into new things. After they have said what they saw, explain: wax is made of carbon and hydrogen. In the flame, the hydrogen joins with oxygen from the air and makes water vapour. The carbon makes invisible carbon dioxide, and a little is left as soot.
flow.context: This is the last step of Catch What a Flame Makes. You say what you found and why.

activities.title: Blue or Yellow? Read the stove flame

materials.item: a gas stove with a burner, turned on by a grown-up
a steel spoon, wet, and a pinch of table salt
a cold steel plate
a tea-light candle, for comparing
paper and coloured pencils

schedule.what: Look at the burner. Light it. Compare the stove flame with the candle. Try the salt. Draw both flames.

activities.safety: A grown-up works the stove and the flame. Keep long hair tied back and sleeves rolled up. Use only a few grains of salt, so the burner holes do not clog. If you have no gas stove, use the candle for all steps.
activities.record: Draw the stove flame and the candle flame side by side, with colours. Write where each one makes soot, and which one has air holes.
activities.context: In this activity, you compare the blue flame of a gas stove with the yellow flame of a candle. You also see how salt changes a flame's colour.

setup.art: An unlit gas stove burner with small air holes at the base, and a child pointing at them.
setup.caption: 1. Before the stove is lit, look closely at the burner. Find the tiny holes.

setup.art: A blue ring of flame on the burner next to a yellow candle flame, with a cold steel plate held above each by an adult.
setup.caption: 2. The grown-up lights the burner. Compare the stove flame with the candle flame.

setup.art: A wet steel spoon dipped in salt held at the edge of the blue flame, where the flame turns bright yellow-orange.
setup.caption: 3. Dip a wet spoon in salt. Hold it at the edge of the flame. Watch the colour change.

flow.do: Look at the unlit burner with your child. Find the small holes around its edge. Ask what they think the holes are for. Write down the guess.
flow.say: Look at the burner before it is lit. Can you find the tiny holes? What do you think they are for? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the burner. Find the tiny holes. What are they for?

ask.q: What do you think comes in through the holes?

flow.parent: The holes let air mix with the gas before it burns, so that there is plenty of oxygen. Do not explain yet. Let your child guess first.
flow.context: This is the first step of reading the stove flame. You look at the burner before you light it.

flow.do: The grown-up lights the burner. Compare its flame with the tea-light. Hold the cold plate for two seconds above each flame. Look at the colour of the stove flame and the candle flame. Look for soot on the plate.
flow.say: What colour is the stove flame? What colour is the candle? Now watch the plate over each one. Which one leaves soot?
flow.kid: Look at the stove flame and the candle flame. Which colour is each? Which leaves soot?

ask.q: Why do you think the candle flame is yellow and the stove flame blue?
good: The candle has soot in it.

flow.parent: The blue flame should leave little or no soot. The yellow candle flame should leave a black patch. A stove flame that is yellow, and that makes the bottoms of pans black, needs its burners cleaned. Ask the gas mechanic to look at it.

check.q: A pan on the stove has a thick black layer on its bottom. What does this most likely mean?
options: The flame has been burning with too little air and making soot
check.why: Soot means some carbon did not burn completely. A blocked burner gives too little air, and the flame turns yellow and sooty. The fix is to get the burners cleaned.

flow.context: In this step, you compare the blue stove flame with the yellow candle flame.

flow.do: Wet the steel spoon. Dip it in a little salt so a few grains stick. Hold the spoon at the edge of the blue flame. Watch the flame near the spoon change colour.
flow.say: Dip a wet spoon into the salt, so a few grains stick. Hold it at the edge of the flame. What colour does the flame turn? Why do you think it changed?
flow.kid: A grown-up holds a salty spoon in the flame. What colour does it turn?

ask.q: What do you think the salt does to the flame?
good: Something in the salt gives light.

flow.parent: The flame near the spoon should flash a bright yellow-orange. That is the colour of sodium, one of the atoms in salt. After they have answered, tell them that every element gives its own colour of light when it is heated. Fireworks use this for their colours.
flow.context: In this step, you see how salt changes the colour of the flame.

activities.title: The Gas Smell Drill: what to do if you smell LPG

materials.item: a cardboard sign or paper with the words stove, regulator and window drawn on it
paper and a pencil to draw the plan
your home's gas regulator and a window or door, for the walk-through

schedule.what: Learn why gas has a smell. Walk through the steps. Practise the drill twice. Write the helpline numbers on the fridge.

activities.record: Write the five steps in order on a card and stick it near the kitchen, with the emergency numbers beside it.
activities.context: In this activity, you learn what to do if you smell cooking gas, and you practise it like a fire drill.

setup.art: A child pointing at the red regulator on a gas cylinder in a kitchen, with an arrow showing it being turned off.
setup.caption: 1. Find the regulator on your gas cylinder. A grown-up shows how to turn it off.

setup.art: A family member opening a kitchen window wide, with arrows showing gas flowing out, and a light switch crossed out beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Open the windows and doors. Do not touch any switches.

setup.art: A child running outside the house while a grown-up holds a phone to call for help.
setup.caption: 3. Go outside. Call for help from outside.

flow.do: Say that cooking gas has no smell of its own, and that a smelly chemical is added on purpose. Ask your child why they think this is done.
flow.say: LPG has no smell by itself. A smelly chemical is added, like rotten eggs. Why do you think the gas company does that?
flow.kid: Gas has no smell. A smell is added. Why?

ask.q: Why would a company add a bad smell to gas?
good: Because we could not tell otherwise.

flow.parent: The smell is a chemical called ethyl mercaptan. It is added so that a leak can be noticed before the gas builds up. Gas mixed with air in the right amounts can catch fire or explode from a single spark.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Gas Smell Drill. You find out why gas smells.

flow.do: Walk through the five steps with your child, in order. First, no flames or switches. Then turn off the regulator, open windows and doors, go outside, and call for help. Let them point at each place as you go.
flow.say: If we smell gas, first we touch no flames and no switches. Then we turn off the regulator, open every window, go outside, and call for help.
flow.kid: No flames. No switches. Turn off the regulator. Open windows. Go outside. Call for help.

ask.q: Why must we not switch on a light when we smell gas?
good: A spark could set the gas on fire.

flow.parent: A switch can make a tiny spark. If gas has built up in the room, that spark can set it off. In India, the LPG emergency number on your cylinder or bill (the national LPG emergency line is 1906) and the fire service (101) are the ones to call, from outside. Check the numbers for your area and write them on the card.

check.q: You smell gas in the kitchen. What should you do first?
options: Not touch any flame or switch, then turn off the regulator and open the windows
Switch on the light to look for the leak
Light a match to see where the smell comes from
check.why: A flame or a spark could set the gas on fire. The safe order is no sparks, regulator off, windows open, then go outside and call for help.

flow.context: In this step, you walk through the five steps in order.

flow.do: Play the drill twice. A grown-up says 'I smell gas.' Your child acts out the steps in order. They point at the regulator and the window. Then swap places, and let the child give the signal.
flow.say: I will say 'I smell gas.' You show me what to do, in order. Point to the regulator. Point to the windows. Then we go outside.
flow.kid: A grown-up says 'I smell gas.' Do the steps in order. Then swap.

ask.q: Which step is the hardest to remember?

flow.parent: Practise this twice a year. Stick the card with the steps and numbers beside the kitchen door. Children who have practised a drill remember it far better in a real moment.
flow.context: In this step, you practise the drill like a fire drill, twice.

projects.title: Pour Out a Fire: make carbon dioxide and put out a candle

materials.item: a tall clear glass jar or bottle with a wide mouth, about 500 millilitres to 1 litre
3 level tablespoons of baking soda
100 millilitres of white vinegar, about half a cup
a tea-light candle standing in the bottom of a deep steel katori or a bowl with tall sides
a tray to catch spills, a spoon, and a towel
matches, for the grown-up only

projects.safety: A grown-up lights the candle. Do not pour the liquid on the candle. Hold the jar tilted only so that the gas pours out, and keep the foam inside. Keep the candle away from curtains and paper.

schedule.what: Guess. Make the gas. Pour it onto the candle. Try again with a fresh jar. Explain what happened.

projects.record: Draw the jar, the candle in the bowl, and an arrow showing the invisible gas pouring. Write why the flame went out.
projects.context: In this project, you make carbon dioxide from baking soda and vinegar, and pour it onto a candle to put out the flame.

setup.art: A tall jar with three spoons of baking soda at the bottom and vinegar being poured in, with bubbles rising.
setup.caption: 1. Put baking soda in the jar. Add vinegar. Watch the fizz.

setup.art: A lit tea-light standing at the bottom of a deep steel katori on a tray.
setup.caption: 2. Stand a lit tea-light in the bottom of a deep bowl.

setup.art: A hand tilting the jar slowly over the deep bowl, with an arrow of invisible gas flowing down into the bowl and the flame going out.
setup.caption: 3. When the fizz has calmed, tilt the jar over the bowl. Pour out only the gas.

flow.do: Show your child the jar, the baking soda, the vinegar and the candle in its bowl. Ask for a guess about what will happen when you tilt the fizzing jar over the flame. Ask for a reason.
flow.say: We will make a gas in the jar. Then we will tilt the jar over the candle, but not pour any liquid. What do you think will happen to the flame? Why?
flow.kid: We make a gas in a jar. We tilt it over a flame. What will happen? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the flame will or will not change?
good: The gas will put it out.
Nothing will happen, as you cannot see the gas.
The gas will make it bigger.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is good. Most children expect nothing, because the gas cannot be seen.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pour Out a Fire. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Put 3 spoons of baking soda in the jar. Pour in 100 millilitres of vinegar. It fizzes. Wait until the fizz calms down, about one minute. Keep the jar upright.
flow.say: Put the baking soda in the jar. Add the vinegar. It fizzes. That fizz is a gas. Wait until it calms down.
flow.kid: Put baking soda in the jar. Add vinegar. Watch it fizz. Wait until it calms.

ask.q: What do you see in the jar? What do you think the bubbles are?

flow.parent: Baking soda and vinegar react and make carbon dioxide. This is a chemical reaction, because a new gas appears and it cannot be turned back. Place the jar on a tray in case the foam rises over the top.

check.q: Why do we say that making the fizz is a chemical reaction?
options: A new gas is made that was not there before
check.why: A new substance, carbon dioxide gas, appears. That is the sign of a chemical reaction. A change in temperature alone is not enough.

flow.context: In this step, you make carbon dioxide gas in the jar.

flow.do: The grown-up stands the tea-light in the deep bowl and lights it. Hold the jar over the bowl. Tilt it slowly, as if pouring water, but keep the liquid in. Stop if the foam reaches the rim.
flow.say: Tilt the jar slowly over the bowl, as if pouring water. Keep the liquid in the jar. Watch the flame. What happens?
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the candle. Tilt the jar like pouring. Keep the liquid in. Watch the flame.

ask.q: What happened to the flame? What was poured out of the jar?

flow.parent: The flame should go out within a few seconds as the gas sinks into the bowl. If it does not, make a fresh jar, tilt it closer to the flame and tilt it more steeply. The candle should sit well below the rim of the bowl so that the gas pools around it.
flow.context: In this step, you pour the gas onto the candle.

flow.do: Light the candle again. Ask your child to explain what happened, and why. Draw the jar and the arrow of gas. Try once more.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think would happen? What did you see? Why do you think the flame went out?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why. Draw the jar and the gas.
flow.think: You cannot see the gas. How do you know it was poured?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the gas was heavier than air, so it poured into the bowl and pushed the air, and the oxygen, away from the flame. After they have said what they saw, explain: carbon dioxide does not burn, and it is heavier than air.
flow.context: This is the last step of Pour Out a Fire. You explain what you saw.

challenges.title: Keep the Flame Going: design a lid with holes for a jar
challenges.problem: A tea-light stands inside a glass jar. Cover the whole mouth of the jar with a lid made of foil and card. Make the lid so that the flame burns for at least two full minutes.
constraints: The lid must cover the whole mouth of the jar, with no big gaps left by folding.
You may use only foil, card, tape and scissors.
The lid may have as many holes and tubes as you like.
A grown-up lights the candle and puts the lid on.
Time the flame with a stopwatch, from putting the lid on until the flame goes out.
materials: a glass jar, about 500 millilitres to 1 litre, with a wide mouth
an incense stick, for the grown-up, to show where the air flows

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to draw two or three different lids, with holes and tubes in different places. Ask for a guess about which will work best.
flow.say: The flame needs fresh air to keep burning. How could you let air in, and let the burnt gas out? Draw a few lids first.
flow.kid: Draw two or three lids. Where should the holes go?

ask.q: Where should air go in, and where should it go out?
good: In at the sides, out at the middle.
Hot gas goes up, so out at the top.

flow.parent: Hot air and gas from a flame rise. This pulls fresh air in from below, if it has a way in. A lid with only one hole makes the air go out and in by the same hole, which does not work well.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Keep the Flame Going challenge. You plan your lids.

flow.do: Make the first lid from foil. A grown-up lights the candle and puts the lid on. Start the timer. Write the time when the flame goes out. Make a change to the lid, and test again. Change only one thing each time.
flow.say: Make your first lid. I will light the candle and put it on. You start the timer. When the flame goes out, write down the time.
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the candle and puts on your lid. Time the flame. Write the time.

ask.q: What did you change between tests? What difference did it make?
good: I added a hole at the edge.

flow.parent: A lid with holes near the edge and one hole in the middle usually lets the flame burn much longer than a lid with a single hole. A rolled card tube over the middle hole often helps further. The jar and foil get hot, so do not touch them until they have cooled. Let the grown-up show the flow of air with a puff of incense smoke near the holes.

check.q: Your flame lasts much longer after you add small holes near the edge of the lid. Why?
options: Fresh air can now flow in, while the hot gas goes out of the middle
The holes make the flame bigger
check.why: A flame needs a steady supply of oxygen. Holes at the edge let fresh air in. The hot gas from the flame rises and leaves through the middle. This flow is the same idea as a chimney.

flow.context: In this step, you build lids, test them with a timer, and change one thing each time.

flow.do: Compare all your lids. Which lasted longest? Why? Draw the best lid, with arrows showing the air going in and out.
flow.say: Look at all the times. Which lid was best? Show me with arrows where the air goes in and where it goes out.
flow.kid: Which lid lasted longest? Draw it. Draw arrows for the air.
flow.think: A chulha has a chimney. How is it like your best lid?
flow.parent: A strong answer says that the best lid lets fresh air in low down and lets hot gas out high up, as a chimney does. This is why a stove with a good chimney burns hotter and makes less smoke.
flow.context: This is the last step of the challenge. You compare your lids and explain the best one.

general: A lid with a hole at the edge and a hole in the middle, so air flows in and out.
A lid with many small holes all round the edge.
A lid with one big hole in the middle only, as the simplest first test.
creative: A lid with a rolled card tube over the middle hole, which works like a chimney.
A card divider in the jar, with fresh air going down one side and hot gas going up the other.
A lid with holes at the edge and a tube that takes the hot gas away, so the jar stays cooler.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your lid design. Build it and time the flame. Change one thing, such as the number of holes, and time it again. Which lid lasted longest? Why do you think that was?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about air and burning. You design a lid that keeps a flame going in a jar.

setup.art: A child sketching three lid designs on paper: one with a single hole, one with edge holes and a middle hole, and one with a card tube.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some lid designs on paper.

setup.art: A foil lid with small holes round the edge, being placed on a jar containing a lit tea-light, with a stopwatch beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Make your lid. A grown-up lights the candle and puts the lid on. Start the timer.

setup.art: Two lids side by side with their times written below, one with 20 seconds and one with 3 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Change one thing at a time, and compare the times.
