quiz.p: Which of these is the best way to describe burning a candle?
opts: The wax joins with oxygen and makes new substances
The wax disappears
The wax melts and evaporates
quiz.why: Burning makes new substances, carbon dioxide and water. Disappearing is not possible, and melting or evaporating alone would leave the wax as wax.

quiz.p: A cold steel spoon is held over a flame and gets drops of water on it. Where did that water come from?
opts: The flame made it from the hydrogen in the fuel and oxygen from the air
The spoon made it
It was inside the candle as liquid water
quiz.why: The hydrogen in the wax joins with oxygen and makes water vapour. The cold spoon turns it back into drops.

quiz.p: Suppose you could weigh a log and the oxygen it uses, and also all the gases and ash it makes. How would the two totals compare?
opts: They would be the same
The second would be smaller, because the fire destroys things
The second would be bigger, because the fire adds new matter
quiz.why: Atoms are rearranged, not made or destroyed. So the total mass is the same before and after.

quiz.p: Which of these will burn fastest?
opts: A heap of thin wood shavings
A thick log
A log wrapped in wet cloth
quiz.why: Thin shavings show a lot of surface to the air, so oxygen reaches the fuel at many places at once.

quiz.p: A flame is yellow and leaves black marks on a pan. What does this tell you about the air supply?
opts: There is too little oxygen, so some carbon is left unburnt as soot
There is too much oxygen
The pan is too hot
quiz.why: A yellow, sooty flame means incomplete burning, from too little oxygen reaching the fuel. A clean blue flame has plenty of oxygen.

quiz.p: Which explanation fits the fact that burnt steel wool is heavier than before?
opts: Iron joined with oxygen from the air, and the oxygen's mass stayed in the solid
The burning made new iron
The ash is heavier than the iron, because ash is always heavy
quiz.why: No new iron can be made. The extra weight is oxygen, now joined to the iron. This was one of Lavoisier's clues.

quiz.p: Burning paper proves that burning always makes things lighter.
quiz.why: False. Paper becomes gases that float away, so the ash is light. Steel wool becomes a solid oxide, so it gets heavier. In both, the oxygen from the air has joined in.

quiz.p: Which of these puts out a small fire of oil in a pan?
opts: Switching off the heat and covering the pan with a lid
Pouring cold water on the pan
Blowing on the pan hard
quiz.why: A lid cuts off the oxygen. Water would sink and turn to steam, and throw burning oil out. Blowing would bring in more oxygen.

quiz.p: The Sun has shone for billions of years. Why can it not be burning like a fire?
opts: A burning Sun would have run out of fuel in a few thousand years, and space has almost no oxygen
The Sun is too bright to burn
The Sun is made of liquid
quiz.why: Burning needs oxygen and would use the Sun up very fast. The Sun shines by fusion, in which hydrogen joins to make helium.

quiz.p: Why was it a puzzle for the phlogiston idea that tin got heavier when it burned?
opts: If burning lets something escape, burnt things should get lighter
Tin does not burn
Phlogiston is heavy
quiz.why: If something left the tin, the tin should weigh less. It weighed more because it took in oxygen from the air.

quiz.p: A pinch of salt turns a flame yellow-orange, because of the element ____ in the salt.
a: sodium
quiz.why: Sodium atoms give out yellow light when they are heated. Every element has its own colours, which lets astronomers read starlight.

quiz.p: You smell cooking gas in the kitchen. What should you do first?
opts: Touch no flame or switch, turn off the regulator, and open the windows
Light a match to find the leak
Switch on the fan to blow the smell away
quiz.why: A flame or a spark from a switch could set the gas on fire. The safe order is no sparks, regulator off, windows open, then go outside and call for help.

items.p: In chemistry, what is burning?
opts: A chemical reaction in which a fuel joins with oxygen and gives out heat and light
A change of state, like melting
A way of making things disappear
items.why: Burning makes new substances, so it is a chemical reaction. Melting changes only the state of a substance. Nothing disappears, as the atoms are only rearranged.

items.p: A cold plate held over a candle flame gets wet because the flame makes ____ vapour.
a: water
items.why: The hydrogen in the wax joins with oxygen and makes water vapour. It turns back into drops when it touches the cold plate.

items.p: When a candle burns away, the wax is destroyed.
items.why: False. The wax turns into water vapour, carbon dioxide and a little soot. They spread through the air. The atoms are all still there.

items.p: Match each clue to what it shows.
pairs: Drops on a cold plate held over a flame
A black patch on a spoon held in a flame
Some carbon did not burn completely, and made soot
Fog on a cold plate when you breathe on it
Your breath holds water vapour too
A blue flame with no soot
items.why: Each clue shows one product of burning, or how complete the burning was. Water vapour turns into drops on cold surfaces, and soot is unburnt carbon.

items.p: Sort each change by whether it makes a new substance.
items.why: Burning and rusting make new substances, because the material joins with oxygen. Melting, boiling and dissolving only change where the particles are or how they sit. The substance is the same.

items.p: The same newspaper is rolled tightly and burned. It burns more slowly than the same paper crumpled loosely. Why?
opts: Less air can reach the paper inside the tight roll
The tight roll is heavier
Rolled paper is made of a different material
items.why: Burning goes on only where oxygen reaches the fuel. In a tight roll, the inside gets little air, so the flame is slower. The paper is the same.

items.p: Put these in the right order, for how thin twigs help to light a thick log.
a: Thin twigs catch fire quickly
The twigs' heat warms the log
The warm log gives out gas that can burn
The log burns with a steady flame
items.why: Thin twigs have a lot of surface, so they catch quickly. Their heat starts the log giving out gas. Once the log's gas burns, the flame feeds itself.

items.p: Why does blowing gently on glowing embers make them glow brighter? Use the word oxygen.
items.a: Blowing brings fresh air to the embers. The air carries oxygen, so the embers burn faster and glow brighter.
items.why: A strong answer says that burning needs oxygen at the surface of the fuel, and that blowing sends in new oxygen. A weaker answer says only that blowing makes the fire bigger.

items.p: A candle flame is yellow, and a clean gas stove flame is blue. What makes the candle flame yellow?
opts: Tiny bits of hot soot glowing inside the flame
Cold water in the flame
The flame is far from the wick
items.why: In the candle, some carbon is not burnt completely. It forms tiny bits of soot, which glow yellow when hot. The stove mixes in air first, so the burning is complete and the flame is blue.

items.p: Carbon monoxide has a strong smell, so you will always notice it.
items.why: False. Carbon monoxide has no colour and no smell. That is why it is dangerous. A coal or charcoal fire must never burn in a closed room.

items.p: A smelly chemical is added to cooking gas so that people can notice a ____.
a: leak
gas leak
items.why: LPG has no smell of its own. The added smell warns people of a leak before the gas builds up.

items.p: A pan of cooking oil catches fire on the stove. What is the safest thing to do?
opts: Switch off the stove and cover the pan with a lid
Throw a glass of water on it
Carry the pan outside
items.why: A lid shuts out oxygen. Water sinks under the oil and turns to steam at once, which throws burning oil around. Carrying a burning pan can spill burning oil on you.

items.p: Draw a candle with a cold plate above it. Draw arrows to show where the water and the soot collect, and label them.
items.a: A candle flame with a plate above it, an arrow to drops of water on the plate's underside, and an arrow to a black patch of soot.
items.why: A strong drawing shows drops of water on the cold plate, soot where the plate touches the yellow tip, and invisible carbon dioxide rising away.

items.p: Here is a picture of a candle flame with three arrows. Label each arrow with one of these products.
a: Arrow to the invisible gas rising: carbon dioxide
Arrow to the drops on the cold plate: water vapour
Arrow to the black patch: soot
items.why: A flame makes two invisible gases and some black soot. Water vapour can be caught as drops on a cold plate, and soot as a black patch.
items.art: A candle flame with a cold plate above it and three empty label boxes next to arrows pointing to drops, a black patch and a rising invisible gas.

items.p: Kavya and Farhan watch a log burn down to a pile of ash.

views.who: Kavya, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The log is gone. All that is left is a little ash.

views.who: Farhan, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The log is not gone. Most of it has gone into the air as gases.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? How could you test it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. It may say that a cold plate over a burning log would catch water, or that weighing the ash and the log shows the rest became gas.
items.why: Both have a point. The log has gone as a log. But the atoms in it have not gone anywhere. They are in the gases, the ash and the soot.

items.p: A bundle of dry coconut fronds weighs 3,000 grams. After burning, 120 grams of ash is left. How many grams of the fronds became gases and soot that floated away?
items.why: 3,000 take away 120 is 2,880. About 2,880 grams of the fronds turned into gases and fine smoke that went into the air.

items.p: A tuft of steel wool is heavier after it has burned. What is the best explanation?
opts: The iron joined with oxygen from the air, and the oxygen is now part of the solid
The fire added new iron
The smoke from the match stuck to it
items.why: Iron is a solid, so nothing floats away. It joins with oxygen from the air and makes a solid oxide. The oxide weighs as much as the iron plus the oxygen.

items.p: A log leaves only a small heap of ash. Where did most of its weight go?
opts: Into gases, such as carbon dioxide and water vapour, in the air
Into nothing at all
Down into the ground
items.why: Wood is mostly carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. These atoms join with oxygen from the air and make gases that float away. Only the minerals stay behind as ash.

items.p: If you could weigh a log and the oxygen it uses, and then all the gas and ash it makes, the totals would be the same.
items.why: True. This is the conservation of mass. The atoms are only rearranged, so none are lost.

items.p: The idea that the total mass stays the same in a chemical reaction is called the conservation of ____.
a: mass
items.why: Lavoisier's careful weighing showed this in the 1770s. It is one of the most tested ideas in science.

items.p: The phlogiston idea could not explain why some burnt metals got heavier.
items.why: True. If burning let something escape, burnt things should get lighter. Tin and iron got heavier, because they took oxygen from the air.

items.p: A candle goes out in a closed jar, though plenty of air is still inside. Why?
opts: The oxygen has fallen too low to keep the flame going, though some is left
The jar is too cold
All the air has been used up
items.why: Air starts with about 21 parts oxygen in every 100. A candle goes out while much of the oxygen is still left. Plenty of air remains, but not enough oxygen.

items.p: Put these in the right order for running a fair test of how shape changes burning speed.
a: Cut every piece of paper to the same size
Make each piece into a different shape
Light each piece in the same way
Time how long each one burns
Compare the times
items.why: A fair test changes only one thing. The paper is the same and the lighting is the same, so only the shape differs. Timing and comparing come last.

items.p: Sort each flame by whether the fuel is burning completely or incompletely.
items: a clean gas stove burner with a blue flame
a candle with a sooty yellow flame
a smoky wood chulha with black smoke
a stove burner with a blue ring and no soot on the pan
a pan blackened by a yellow stove flame
a Bunsen burner with its air hole fully open
items.why: Blue flames with no soot show that the fuel has plenty of air and burns completely. Yellow flames and black smoke show soot, which means some carbon did not burn completely.

items.p: A family burns charcoal in a closed room to keep warm. What is the main danger?
opts: A poisonous gas with no smell, called carbon monoxide, builds up
The room will get too bright
The charcoal will burn too slowly
items.why: Charcoal burns incompletely in a room with little air, and makes carbon monoxide. It has no colour and no smell, so a person cannot tell it is there.

items.p: A neighbour says: 'If there is no smoke, it is safe to burn charcoal in a closed room.' Do you agree? Why?
items.a: No. Carbon monoxide has no colour, no smell and no smoke, but it is poisonous. A fire in a closed room can make it even when you see nothing.
items.why: A strong answer says that the dangerous gas is invisible and has no smell. The lack of smoke does not mean the room is safe.

items.p: Water is the best way to put out a burning pan of oil.
items.why: False. Oil floats on water. Water thrown on burning oil sinks, turns to steam at once, and throws the burning oil outwards. Cover the pan with a lid.

items.p: Carbon dioxide can put out a candle, though you cannot see it. How?
opts: It is heavier than air, so it pours down and pushes the oxygen away from the flame
It makes the candle colder
It is a kind of water
items.why: Carbon dioxide does not burn, and it is heavier than air. When poured over a flame, it pushes the air away and cuts off the oxygen.

items.p: Nila and Hari are talking about the Sun on a hot afternoon.

views.who: Nila, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The Sun is a giant fire. That is why it is so hot and bright.

views.who: Hari, a boy in Class 4 (an imagined view)
views.says: The Sun is not burning. There is almost no oxygen in space, so it must work in a different way.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What evidence would settle it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks Hari's side. It notes that burning needs oxygen, and that a burning Sun would run out in a few thousand years, while the Sun has shone for billions of years.
items.why: Hari is right. The Sun runs on fusion, not burning. Nila is right that the Sun is hot and bright, but a fire could not last as long as the Sun has.

items.p: A jar holds 500 millilitres of air. About one fifth of air is oxygen. How many millilitres of oxygen are in the jar?
items.why: One fifth of 500 is 500 divided by 5, which is 100. So the jar holds about 100 millilitres of oxygen.

items.p: Draw the steel wool balance at three moments: before burning, while it burns, and after it has cooled. Show which side is lower each time.
items.a: Three drawings of a skewer hung from its middle. Before: level. While burning: level or nearly. After cooling: the burnt side lower.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the balance level at the start, and the burnt side lower at the end, because the burnt wool is heavier.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Rusting, a cut apple turning brown, a candle burning, wax melting.
items.a: Wax melting, because it makes no new substance. The other three are the wax, iron or apple joining with oxygen.
items.why: Rusting, browning and burning all make new substances with oxygen. Melting changes only the state, so the wax is still wax.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a gas stove burner. Label the three parts that matter for a blue flame.
a: The small holes at the base of the burner: air holes
The pipe that leads to the burner: gas coming in
The ring of flame above the burner: blue flame
items.why: Air comes in through the holes and mixes with the gas before it burns. With plenty of oxygen, the carbon burns completely and the flame is blue.
items.art: A gas stove burner seen from the side, with a pipe underneath, small holes at the base, a blue ring of flame, and three empty label boxes.

items.p: A friend says: 'Fire destroys things.' Use burning steel wool or a candle to show what is wrong with this idea.
items.a: Steel wool gets heavier when it burns, so something was added, not lost. A candle flame leaves water and soot on a cold plate, so the wax changed into new things. Burning rearranges atoms and does not destroy them.
items.why: A strong answer uses one piece of evidence, such as the heavier steel wool or the drops on a cold plate, and says what it shows.

items.p: Burning paper seems to get lighter, but burning steel wool gets heavier. Explain both with one idea.
items.a: In both, the material joins with oxygen. Paper becomes gases that float away, so the ash is light. Iron becomes a solid oxide that stays behind, so it holds the oxygen's weight.
items.why: A strong answer says that the oxygen joins in both cases, and that what differs is whether the new substance is a gas that escapes or a solid that stays.

items.p: A candle loses 12 grams of wax as it burns. The oxygen it uses weighs 36 grams. How many grams of gases and soot does it make?
items.why: Everything the wax and oxygen weighed must still be there. 12 plus 36 is 48. So the new gases and soot weigh 48 grams.

items.p: A tea-light stands on a kitchen scale inside a sealed jar. The scale shows 400 grams. The flame burns until it goes out. What will the scale show now?
opts: 400 grams, because nothing has got out of the jar
Less than 400 grams, because the wax was destroyed
More than 400 grams, because the flame added weight
items.why: The wax joined with oxygen inside the sealed jar, and nothing escaped. The new gases weigh as much as the wax and the oxygen that went in.

items.p: A cloud of flour dust in a mill can burn in a flash, but a heap of flour on a shelf does not. Why?
opts: The dust has far more surface touching the air, so it burns far faster
The dust is hotter
The dust is a different kind of food
items.why: Burning goes on only where oxygen touches the fuel. A cloud of dust shows a huge surface to the air, so it can burn in a flash. A heap shows only its outside.

items.p: A village is deciding how to cook. Some use wood fires in the kitchen. Others have an LPG stove.

views.who: Meera, a girl in Class 4 (an imagined view)

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What would you want to find out first?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer weighs cost against health, and notes that incomplete burning in a closed kitchen makes smoke and carbon monoxide. It may ask who pays for gas, and who breathes the smoke.
items.why: Both have a point. Wood is cheap, but incomplete burning gives smoke, soot and carbon monoxide. A cleaner fire needs better air supply, a chimney, or a different fuel.

items.p: Put these in the right order, to show how the energy in a log came from the Sun.
a: A leaf catches sunlight
The plant builds wood from air and water
The wood is burned in a fire
The fire warms a room
items.why: A leaf uses sunlight to make wood. Burning gives the stored energy back as heat and light.

items.p: Match each element to the colour it gives a flame.
items.why: Atoms of each element give out their own colours of light when heated. That is why fireworks have different colours.

items.p: The light from a star can tell us which elements are in it.
items.why: True. Each element gives its own colours of light. Astronomers split starlight into colours and match them to elements, as with a flame at home.

items.p: Why can the Sun not be burning like a fire?
opts: There is almost no oxygen in space, and a burning Sun would have run out of fuel in a few thousand years
The Sun is too far away
The Sun is made of water
items.why: Burning needs oxygen, and a burning Sun would last only a few thousand years. The Sun has shone for about 4.6 billion years, because it runs on fusion.

items.p: On the space station, a candle flame is a small blue ball, not a teardrop. Explain why, using the words hot gas and rise.
items.a: On Earth, hot gas is lighter and rises, so the flame stretches into a teardrop, and fresh air flows in from below. In weightlessness, hot gas does not rise, so the flame stays round and gets fresh air only by slow drifting.
items.why: A strong answer says that rising hot gas is what pulls the flame into a teardrop on Earth, and that weightlessness removes this.

items.p: Draw wax atoms and oxygen atoms before burning, and carbon dioxide and water after burning. Use circles for atoms and show that none are lost.
items.a: A drawing with carbon, hydrogen and oxygen circles joined in groups on the left. On the right, the same circles in new groups, carbon dioxide and water, with the same number of each kind of circle.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the same number of each kind of atom before and after, only grouped differently.

items.p: In a chemical reaction the atoms are rearranged, but none are ____.
a: lost
destroyed
items.why: The atoms that start the reaction are all still there at the end. They have only changed partners.

items.p: Both your body's cells and a candle flame take in oxygen. What do both of them give out?
opts: Carbon dioxide and water
Pure oxygen
Only heat
items.why: Cells break down food with oxygen and make carbon dioxide and water. A flame does the same with wax. The body does it slowly and in small steps.

items.p: Which one is not a case of burning? An oil lamp, a chulha, the Sun, a sparkler.
items.a: The Sun, because it shines by fusion and not by burning. The other three join a fuel with oxygen.
items.why: An oil lamp, a chulha and a sparkler all burn fuel in oxygen. The Sun has almost no oxygen, and its energy comes from fusion.

items.p: Here is a picture of a jar with a lid that has holes. Label what happens at each arrow.
a: Arrow into the edge holes: fresh air in
Arrow out of the middle hole: hot gas out
The tea-light: flame
items.why: A flame burns longest when fresh air can flow in and the hot gas can flow out. The hot gas rises, and so pulls in fresh air.

open_questions.q: How do cool flames burn fuel without a visible flame, and can they be used in cleaner engines?
open_questions.why_open: Cool flames were only seen clearly in space experiments around 2012. Scientists are still working out the reactions inside them.

open_questions.q: Is a flame a plasma, or only a hot glowing gas?
open_questions.why_open: A flame holds a tiny share of charged particles. Whether that is enough to call it a plasma depends on where you draw the line, and scientists draw it in different places.

open_questions.q: How exactly do soot particles form inside a flame?
open_questions.why_open: Soot forms from small molecules joining into large ones in a few thousandths of a second. The exact steps are very hard to follow, and are still being studied.

open_questions.q: When did people first learn to make fire, and not only keep it going?
open_questions.why_open: Fire leaves little behind. Ash and charcoal rot or blow away, so the earliest evidence is rare and hard to date.

open_questions.q: Can we find ways to burn fuel for energy without adding extra carbon dioxide to the air?
open_questions.why_open: There are many ideas, from new fuels to catching carbon dioxide, but none yet works everywhere at low cost.

maths.problem: In the paper test, Meena timed the flat sheet at 9 seconds and 11 seconds, and the tight roll at 41 seconds and 47 seconds. What is the average time for each shape? How many times longer does the roll take than the flat sheet?
maths.answer: Flat: 10 seconds. Roll: 44 seconds. The roll takes 4.4 times as long.
maths.explain: Flat: 9 plus 11 is 20, and 20 divided by 2 is 10. Roll: 41 plus 47 is 88, and 88 divided by 2 is 44. Then 44 divided by 10 is 4.4.
maths.why_maths: An average of two tries is more trustworthy than one try. Dividing the averages shows how big the difference is.

maths.problem: A tuft of steel wool weighs 4 grams. After burning, it weighs 5 grams. What fraction and what percentage of its original weight did it gain?
maths.explain: It gained 5 take away 4, which is 1 gram. One gram out of 4 grams is 1 over 4. One quarter is 25 percent.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare how much weight different tufts gain, even when the tufts are different sizes.

maths.problem: A bundle of fronds weighs 3,000 grams and leaves 120 grams of ash. What percentage of the weight was left as ash?
maths.explain: 120 out of 3,000 is 120 over 3,000. Dividing top and bottom by 30 gives 4 over 100. That is 4 percent.
maths.why_maths: A percentage shows how small the ash is compared with the fuel, and so how much must have gone into the air.

maths.problem: A gas burner burns 44 grams of propane with 160 grams of oxygen. It makes 132 grams of carbon dioxide and 72 grams of water. Check that the total mass is the same before and after.
maths.answer: Before: 204 grams. After: 204 grams. They match.
maths.explain: Before: 44 plus 160 is 204. After: 132 plus 72 is 204. The totals are equal, so no mass has been lost.
maths.why_maths: Adding up the masses before and after is how chemists check that no atoms are lost in a reaction.

maths.problem: If the Sun were a ball of coal burning, it would last about 5,000 years. The Sun has really shone for about 4,600,000,000 years. About how many times longer is that?
maths.explain: 4,600,000,000 divided by 5,000 is 920,000. So the Sun has lasted nearly a million times longer than a coal Sun could.
maths.why_maths: Dividing two big numbers shows how big the gap is. It shows why the Sun cannot be burning.

maths.problem: An LPG cylinder holds 14.2 kilograms of gas. A family uses about 0.4 kilograms a day. About how many days will it last?
maths.explain: 14.2 divided by 0.4 is the same as 142 divided by 4, which is 35.5. So it lasts about 35 days.
maths.why_maths: Fuel is stored energy, and dividing the amount by the daily use tells a family when they must order the next cylinder.

maths.problem: A tea-light holds 12 grams of wax and burns steadily for 4 hours. Each gram of wax makes about 3 grams of carbon dioxide. How many grams of wax burn in an hour? How many grams of carbon dioxide does the tea-light make in the 4 hours?
maths.answer: 3 grams of wax an hour. About 36 grams of carbon dioxide.
maths.explain: 12 divided by 4 is 3 grams an hour. 12 times 3 is 36 grams of carbon dioxide. The gas weighs three times as much as the wax, because the wax has joined with oxygen.
maths.why_maths: The numbers show that the carbon dioxide weighs more than the wax. It is proof that oxygen from the air has joined in.

maths.problem: In the jar lid challenge, lid A kept the flame going for 20 seconds, lid B for 1 minute 15 seconds, and lid C for 2 minutes 5 seconds. How much longer did lid C last than lid A?
maths.explain: Lid B is 75 seconds and lid C is 125 seconds. 125 take away 20 is 105 seconds. That is 1 minute 45 seconds.
maths.why_maths: Changing minutes and seconds into seconds makes it easy to compare which lid worked best.

roots.context: We have caught what a flame makes, tested how fast things burn, and weighed burning steel wool. Now we ask what burning tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A burning candle does not vanish. It turns into water and gases that spread through the air. A cold plate over the flame catches some of it as drops and soot. Burning swaps the partners of the same atoms, and none is lost.
deep_truth.habit: We say that fire 'uses up' or 'burns away' things, as if burning ended them. That mixes up what we can no longer see with what is no longer there. Gases are invisible, so we think the matter has gone.
deep_truth.evidence: In Catch What a Flame Makes, a cold steel plate held over a tea-light was wet with drops and marked with soot. In the steel wool test, the burning side got heavier, because it took in oxygen from the air.

three.who_am_i: The carbon in your body was once in the air as carbon dioxide, and your breath sends some of it back. You are also part of this swapping of partners.
three.what_is_life: Your cells combine food and oxygen, and make carbon dioxide and water. A living body does a slow version of what a flame does fast.
three.what_is_this_world: The air, the plants, the fires and the animals share the same carbon, passing it round and round. Nothing in this cycle is added and nothing is lost.

roots.thread: A log, a candle and a body all hold carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. In a flame, the atoms leave their old partners and join with oxygen, and become carbon dioxide and water. The same atoms are still there, but they are now invisible and spread out. Plants collect them again from the air and build wood and sugar. So fire is not an ending. It is one step in a circle that carries the same atoms between air, plants, animals and flames.

science.text: In a chemical reaction, the total mass of what goes in equals the total mass of what comes out. This is the conservation of mass.
A fire gives out a tiny amount of mass as heat and light, about a fifth of a millionth of a gram for each kilogram of wood. This follows from E equals m c squared.

other_view.view: The atoms are kept, but the candle is not. A candle, a letter or a forest is a pattern, and patterns really do end. Saying that nothing is lost can hide the fact that something people cared about has gone.

how_we_found_out.story: For about a hundred years, many chemists believed that something escapes from every burning thing. Around 1700, Georg Stahl called it phlogiston. Wood burns, they said, because it gives out phlogiston, and what is left is ash. But there was a puzzle. When metals such as tin or iron burned, the crust that was left weighed more, not less. In the 1770s, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier began weighing everything, even the air. He heated tin inside a sealed glass flask and weighed the whole flask before and after. The weight did not change, and air rushed in when he opened it. The tin had taken something out of the air. Lavoisier named it oxygen. His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, drew his apparatus, kept the laboratory notebooks, and translated English chemistry papers for him. Burning, they showed, is joining with oxygen, not letting something escape.
how_we_found_out.who: Antoine Lavoisier and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier in Paris, building on Georg Stahl's phlogiston and on the oxygen made by Joseph Priestley and Carl Scheele
how_we_found_out.when: About 1700 (phlogiston), 1774 (the sealed flask), 1777 onwards (the name oxygen), 1789 (Lavoisier's book)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Chemists believed that burning lets an invisible substance called phlogiston escape. Burning metals gaining weight did not fit. Lavoisier showed that the metal was joining with oxygen from the air, by weighing everything in a sealed flask.
